edition.note: Seed apparatus. It was machine-drafted and has not yet been checked against the sources: every attribution of a reading to a witness is marked unverified until someone has the book or manuscript in hand. Voices marked illustrative are invented, to show how the form works; they are not real scholars.

witnesses.title: Fair copy with “Grand go the Years”
witnesses.creator: Emily Dickinson
witnesses.context: A fair copy in Dickinson's hand of the revised poem: the first stanza with “Lie”, the “Grand go the Years” stanza and, below a ruled line, the opening of the alternative “Springs — shake the Sills”. The seed file reproduced this page under the name of Fascicle 6, the 1859 copy; it is not that copy, since it does not carry “Light laughs the breeze”. It is probably the later fascicle copy of 1861, which should be confirmed and cited.

image.alt: Manuscript page in Dickinson's hand: the poem with the stanza beginning “Grand go the Years”, followed below a ruled line by the first three lines of “Springs — shake the Sills”.
image.credit: Courtesy Houghton Library, Harvard University. Image used under CC BY-NC-ND 3.0.

witnesses.title: Fascicle 6
witnesses.creator: Emily Dickinson, fair copy
witnesses.citation: Houghton Library, Harvard University, MS Am 1118.3 (h11b–c)
witnesses.context: The earliest extant copy of Fr124, bound by Dickinson herself into Fascicle 6 in late 1859. The page documents her line breaks at "Alabaster" and "members" (split across lines), her indentation of even-numbered lines, and an in-manuscript variant for the word "cadence" (with "cadences" noted as alternate). It is the textual ground from which every subsequent version of the poem departs.

witnesses.title: Susan Dickinson to Emily Dickinson
witnesses.quote: I am not suited, dear Emily with the second verse — It is remarkable as the chain lightening that blinds us hot nights in the Southern sky but it does not go with the ghostly shimmer of the first verse as well as the other one.
witnesses.context: Sue's surviving criticism of the "Crescent" second stanza. She admires it — calls it "remarkable as the chain lightening" — but objects that it does not match the tone of the first verse. She prefers "the other one" — the earlier "Light laughs the breeze" — on grounds of coherence with the first stanza's ghostly cold.

witnesses.title: Emily Dickinson to Susan Dickinson: “Is this frostier?”
witnesses.context: Dickinson's accompanying note when she sent Sue the next attempt — the "Springs — shake the Sills" version. The question is direct evidence that she was responding to Sue's objection that the Crescent stanza did not match the ghostly cold of the first. Three words; an entire revision history hangs from them.

witnesses.title: “Springs — shake the seals” (further revision)
witnesses.context: The document that carries the “seals” stanza. The seed file described the stanza but did not identify the manuscript; until it is identified and cited, this witness is a placeholder.

witnesses.title: Emily Dickinson to T. W. Higginson
witnesses.context: Dickinson's first letter to Thomas Wentworth Higginson enclosed a copy of the poem carrying the “Grand go the Years” stanza: the version she chose to introduce herself to a prospective literary adviser, after Sue had already objected to it.

witnesses.title: Springfield Daily Republican, “The Sleeping”
witnesses.summary: Printed anonymously as "The Sleeping" with the Fascicle 6 stanza ("Light laughs the breeze"). Apparently from the now-lost copy to Susan Dickinson.
witnesses.context: The first time the poem reached print. The newspaper used the Fascicle 6 version of the second stanza, not the Crescent version Dickinson had been working toward. It is possible Sue forwarded the copy; Dickinson seems to have had no editorial say.

positions.label: Lie

attestations.note: Read from the facsimile reproduced on this site.

positions.note: The seed file called this a conjecture that no witness supports. It is in Dickinson's own hand on the manuscript page reproduced here: her revised copy begins the line “Lie the meek members of the Resurrection”. It is an authorial variant, not a conjecture.

voices.name: D. Chen · Yale
voices.reasoning: The sound case is real. "Lie the meek members" is consonantally heavier, matching the stillness the stanza describes. "Sleep" is too soft.

positions.label: Grand go the Years
positions.text:
Grand go the Years,
In the Crescent above them —
Worlds scoop their Arcs —
And Firmaments — row —
Diadems — drop —
And Doges — surrender —
Soundless as Dots,
On a Disc of Snow.

attestations.note: Read from the facsimile reproduced on this site. The lineation and pointing printed here are the seed file's, not the manuscript's.

positions.note: The cosmic stanza Dickinson sent to Thomas Wentworth Higginson in her first letter (April 1862) — empires falling, "Diadems" dropping, "Doges" surrendering, the whole human-political scale reduced to "Dots on a Disc of Snow." The version she chose to introduce herself to a prospective literary advisor; a strong statement of authorial preference, though one Sue had already objected to.

voices.name: J. Park · Brown
voices.reasoning: The version Dickinson chose for Higginson — the strongest single statement of authorial preference in this textual history. The cosmic scale completes what "Alabaster" begins.

positions.label: Light laughs the breeze
positions.text:
Light laughs the breeze
In her Castle above them —
Babbles the Bee in a stolid ear,
Pipe the Sweet Birds in ignorant cadence —
Ah, what sagacity perished here!
positions.note: The second stanza as bound in Fascicle 6 in Dickinson's hand. This is also the version that the Springfield Republican printed (under the title "The Sleeping") on 1 March 1862, presumably from a now-lost copy that had passed through Sue. The stanza places natural life — breeze, bee, birds — against the silence of the entombed, ending in the sharp ironic outcry "Ah, what sagacity perished here!"

voices.name: M. Stein · Wesleyan
voices.reasoning: Bound in Dickinson's own hand into the fascicle. The deliberate copy, not the correspondence draft.

positions.label: Springs — shake the Sills
positions.text:
Springs — shake the Sills —
But — the Echoes — stiffen —
Hoar — is the Window —
and numb — the Door —
Tribes of Eclipse — in Tents of Marble —
Staples of Ages — have buckled — there —

attestations.note: Read from the facsimile reproduced on this site. The page shown breaks off after the first three lines.

positions.note: The "frostier" attempt. The stanza brings the temporal world back into the crypt itself: spring shakes the sills but the echoes do not stir; the window is hoar, the door numb. The structural move is closer to Sue's wish than either of the first two stanzas. Whether Sue accepted it is not recorded.

voices.name: A. Okonkwo · King's College
voices.reasoning: Emily's "Is this frostier?" is the most direct statement of authorial intent we have. She wrote it for this version, in response to Sue.

voices.name: D. Chen · Yale
voices.reasoning: "Hoar — is the Window — / and numb — the Door —" brings the cold inside the structure. It does what the other versions only describe.

positions.label: Springs — shake the seals
positions.text:
Springs — shake the seals —
But the silence — stiffens —
Frosts unhook — in Northern Zones —
Icicles — crawl from polar Caverns —
Midnight in Marble —
Refutes — the Suns —
positions.note: A further revision in which "Sills" becomes the uncapitalised "seals" and the domestic conceit of door-and-window gives way to polar caverns and crawling icicles. The final line — "Midnight in Marble — Refutes — the Suns —" — is one of Dickinson's most uncompromising. Whether this stanza is the further refinement of the previous or an alternative to it remains an open scholarly question.

voices.name: T. Hassan · NYU
voices.reasoning: "Midnight in Marble — Refutes — the Suns —" is the harshest line Dickinson wrote on this material. This version finishes the poem's argument.
